ThingDef.label: The Art of Shin (心)
ThingDef.description:
A hefty hardcover tome, its askew pages patently photocopied from an original manuscript. A large red label pasted onto the cover assigns it as 'CONTRABAND' designated for shredding. The inner side of the back cover has wires running up through it, no doubt an insurance device. Opening this book will allow for only a quick skim before it self destructs.

The first page, in elegant brushstroke handwriting, titles the manuscript 'On The Art of Shin (心) and its Techniques'.

The author prefaces the book with the definition of the technique and its applications, describing Shin (心) as the art of clearing the mind so that it may be sowed with the heaviest of recollections and serve as fertile ground for one's heart to bloom outward. Projecting one's heart in such a manner permits the individual to supercede their physical limitations to a level on par with augmented shock troopers. They describe Shin (心) as a great equalizer of forces, allowing the oppressed to outmatch the oppressor through sheer projection of will alone. The first chapters concern methods and medidations to manifest Shin (心), a process it describes as mentally and spiritually straining. Shin (心) cannot be simply cultivated and must be practically applied in gruesome, life-or-death combat to be mastered. An entire page is dedicated to the phrase "One must endure untold hardship to hone their heart.", followed by several blank pages.

In visibly rougher brushstrokes, the next chapter introduces the concept of Mang (望), a facet within the wider technique of Shin (心). As the individual strengthens their mind, they are able to endure the strain necessary to project their resolve into rings of light that weigh the striking hand, the pull of the trigger, the swing of a sword and greatly augment their power. Mang (望) is described as taking an even greater toll on the mind than Shin (心) to conjure even a single ring. The author warns the reader of the dangers of manifesting Mang (望) and how easily it could push someone unprepared to despair. "Steel your spirit first", it advises.

The handwriting grows even harsher as the author recounts their journey toward honing Shin (心) and Mang (望). It stops instructing and begins reading like a journal on the untold loss they've endured, the countless battles for the sovereignty of their planet and survival of their clan. At the moment of writing they claim to be able to conjure up to three rings and theorize that, although theoretically it has no real limit, a typical human being would be able to endure the strain of a maximum seven rings at a time. They vow to achieve that. The previously elegant brushstrokes have vanished into wild scrawlings and nonsensical ramblings about sin and sunlight.

The last pages handwriting is utterly indecipherable, warping around like beams of light around glyphs of the sun.
